chunks.text: 2.1 Foundation Models for Medical Image Segmentation Vision foundation models provide two complementary components relevant to medical segmentation. DINOv2 and DINOv3 learn transferable visual representations through large-scale self-supervised pretraining, producing spatially dense features that generalize across imaging domains without task-specific supervision Oquab et al. (2023) ; Siméoni et al. (2025) . Beyond pretraining objectives, these dense representations have been directly adopted as frozen visual encoders for downstream segmentation: Li et al. integrate a frozen DINOv3 backbone into an encoder–decoder architecture that achieves competitive performance across seven medical imaging modalities Li et al. (2025) . Zhang et al. adapt vision foundation models as efficient encoders for real-time ultrasound image segmentation Zhang et al. (2025b) . And Ayzenberg et al. augment a prototypical network with a frozen DINOv2 encoder to generate coarse segmentation priors for SAM-guided one-shot adaptation Ayzenberg et al. (2025) . SAM and SAM2 instead provide promptable segmentation architectures, with SAM2 introducing a native memory mechanism for conditioning predictions on previously encoded observations Kirillov and others (2023) ; Ravi et al. (2024) . Medical variants such as MedSAM and MedSAM2 adapt these models through domain-specific training, while parameter-efficient approaches reduce the number of updated model parameters Ma et al. (2024) ; Ma et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2025a) . Zhao et al. further combined both components, encoding support images through a frozen DINOv2 retrieval encoder and storing the resulting representations in the SAM2 memory pathway for training-free few-shot segmentation Zhao et al. (2025) . However, existing approaches primarily achieve task adaptation through parameter optimization, prompt-based conditioning, or retrieval of annotated support examples.

In contrast to retrieval-based methods that use memory primarily for few-shot inference, MemSeg-Agent treats the native SAM2 memory space as a persistent adaptation state. Specifically, it integrates learnable static memory for supervised adaptation, retrieved few-shot memory, and feedback-driven working memory within a unified representation space, while keeping the pretrained segmentation backbone fixed. 3 Method Figure 1: Overview of the MemSeg-Agent framework. Top: Few-shot and test-time working-memory pathways. Few-shot examples are encoded into reusable memory representations, while human corrections during deployment are encoded as delta updates to a test-time working-memory buffer and retrieved according to similarity. Middle: Reference inference pathway. Given an input image, the agentic memory controller retrieves and composes relevant memories from different sources to condition the frozen SAM2-based segmentation backbone for mask prediction. Bottom: Static-memory construction and federated/local training. Static memories are learned offline from pseudo-observations and retrieved for inference, while their representations can be optimized with memory-only communication under the segmentation objective. 3.1 Problem Formulation Let 𝒟 = { ( x i , y i ) } i = 1 N \mathcal{D}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} denote a medical image segmentation dataset, where x i x_{i} is an input image and y i ∈ { 0 , 1 } H × W y_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{H\times W} is the corresponding binary segmentation mask. Memory-space adaptation is consequently characterized by an evolving memory state while the segmentation backbone remains unchanged over time. 3.2 Framework Overview We propose MemSeg-Agent , a memory-augmented segmentation framework built upon a frozen SAM2-family backbone (Fig. 1 ), where adaptation is performed entirely in memory space rather than through repeated model-parameter updates. The framework consists of three complementary memory sources: static memory learned from supervised data to encode stable task-specific priors, few-shot memory constructed directly from labeled support examples, and test-time working memory that accumulates deployment-time corrections. These memory sources share a common SAM2-compatible representation and are coordinated by an Agentic Memory Controller , which retrieves, composes, and updates memory according to the current input and deployment state. The following sections describe static-memory construction, few-shot memory, test-time working-memory adaptation, and the read–write controller in detail. 3.3 Static Memory via Supervision SAM2 defines a memory representation space through its pretrained memory encoder. Given an image–mask pair ( x i , y i ) (x_{i},y_{i}) , the frozen image encoder ℰ I \mathcal{E}_{I} and memory encoder ℰ m \mathcal{E}_{m} produce a SAM2-compatible memory: m i = ℰ m ​ ( ℰ I ​ ( x i ) , y i ) . m_{i}=\mathcal{E}_{m}\bigl(\mathcal{E}_{I}(x_{i}),y_{i}\bigr). (4) To learn task-specific priors without modifying the backbone, we parameterize static memory using learnable pseudo-observations z i = ( x ^ i , y ^ i ) z_{i}=(\hat{x}_{i},\hat{y}_{i}) . A pseudo-observation is a learnable image–mask prototype rather than a real sample or pseudo-label. It is passed through the frozen observation-to-memory pathway to preserve compatibility with SAM2 memory attention.

Given a supervised dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , only the pseudo-observations are optimized: min { z i } i = 1 N ⁡ ℒ seg ​ ( f θ ​ ( x , ∅ , { ℰ m ​ ( ℰ I ​ ( x ^ i ) , y ^ i ) } i = 1 N ) , y ) , θ ​ fixed , \min_{\{z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{seg}}\left(f_{\theta}\left(x,\varnothing;\{\mathcal{E}_{m}(\mathcal{E}_{I}(\hat{x}_{i}),\hat{y}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}\right),y\right),\qquad\theta\ \mathrm{fixed}, (5) where N N is fixed to the memory-bank size. We use slice-wise binary segmentation with Dice Loss plus an auxiliary objectness BCE on foreground-presence logits ℒ seg = ℒ Dice ​ ( y ^ , y ) + 0.3 ​ ℒ BCE ​ ( o ^ , o ) , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{seg}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Dice}}(\hat{y},y)+0.3\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BCE}}(\hat{o},o), (6) where o o and o ^ \hat{o} denote the foreground-presence label and corresponding objectness prediction. In federated settings, each client optimizes the same static-memory variables on local data, and the server consolidates them via FedAvg aggregation. Because only these compact memory variables are transmitted, the frozen foundation model stays local and unchanged. 3.4 Few-shot Memory When labeled data is scarce, directly learning static memory may overfit. Retrieval-augmented few-shot segmentation Zhao et al. (2025) can be integrated into the same memory interface. Given a support set 𝒮 = { ( x i s , y i s ) } i = 1 K \mathcal{S}=\{(x_{i}^{s},y_{i}^{s})\}_{i=1}^{K} , each support pair is encoded into memory through the frozen image and memory encoders. A frozen retrieval encoder ranks support examples according to their similarity to the query image. The top- k k corresponding memories are then used to condition the frozen backbone. Few-shot memory is therefore non-parametric and requires neither fine-tuning nor additional optimization. 3.5 Test-time Working Memory Static memory provides a stable supervised prior, which however may become insufficient when the deployment distribution differs substantially from the training domain.

We therefore introduce test-time working memory to convert clinician feedback into reusable target-domain experience. Unlike conventional test-time adaptation, the segmentation backbone is not optimized during deployment. This adaptation process is activated only when a clinician inspects the current prediction and provides an explicit correction, which is then encoded and incorporated into working memory for future inference. For each target case x t x_{t} , MemSeg-Agent first produces a prediction using only the memory state available before case t t is processed. The clinician then determines whether the segmentation is satisfactory. If a correction is required, a corrected annotation y t ∗ y_{t}^{*} is provided and passed to the memory controller for subsequent memory storage and consolidation. Importantly, the correction is introduced only after the prediction for case t t has been evaluated and therefore cannot improve the result of the same case. The updated working memory can consequently influence only future cases t ′ > t t^{\prime}>t , yielding a strict prequential evaluation protocol that avoids information leakage from current-case corrections. We denote the clinician correction decision by c t ∈ { 0 , 1 } c_{t}\in\{0,1\} . In prospective deployment, c t c_{t} is determined entirely by the clinician and does not require access to ground truth. For retrospective evaluation, we simulate this interaction using a predefined oracle criterion: c t = 𝕀 [ Dice ( y ^ t , y t ) < τ corr ] , c_{t}=\mathbb{I}\left[\mathrm{Dice}(\hat{y}_{t},y_{t})<\tau_{\mathrm{corr}}\right], (7) where τ corr \tau_{\mathrm{corr}} is a predefined performance threshold used to simulate clinician dissatisfaction in retrospective evaluation. When c t = 1 c_{t}=1 , the ground-truth mask is used as a surrogate clinician-corrected annotation in the retrospective experiments.

The threshold therefore serves only to simulate clinician dissatisfaction during retrospective evaluation; it is not an automatic gate required during real deployment. After a correction is provided, the resulting observation is incorporated into the working-memory buffer according to the read–write controller described in Section 3.6 . This buffer persists across sequential target cases and can be retained after deployment as a domain-specific memory bank for future inference. In this way, each clinician intervention is transformed into reusable target-domain experience that can accumulate over time and improve subsequent cases, allowing adaptation knowledge to evolve entirely within the external memory state without gradient-based updates to the segmentation backbone. 3.6 Agentic Memory Controller The Agentic Memory Controller governs how available memory sources are retrieved and composed for prediction, as well as how newly corrected observations are incorporated into persistent working memory. It does not determine whether a clinician correction is required for a given case. Instead, the controller implements the read–write policy that coordinates static, few-shot, and test-time working memories and manages their interaction across a sequential stream of target cases. Consequently, the controller separates stable source knowledge from continuously evolving deployment experience: during reading operation, it preserves the static-memory anchor while selectively retrieving and integrating relevant target-domain information for prediction; and during writing operation, it determines whether newly acquired clinician feedback should expand the working-memory buffer or be consolidated into an existing persistent entry. 4 Experiments 4.1 Datasets and Preprocessing We evaluate the proposed framework on four public datasets covering abdominal MRI, cardiac MRI, and echocardiography. CHAOS Kavur et al. (2021) provides abdominal MRI with left kidney(LK), right kidney(RK), spleen(Spl.), and liver(Liv.) annotations. ACDC Bernard et al.

(2018) contains cardiac MRI with right ventricle (RV), myocardium (Myo), and left ventricle (LV) annotations at end-diastole (ED) and end-systole (ES). CAMUS Leclerc et al. (2019b) consists of two- and four-chamber echocardiographic views with LV, Myo, and left atrium (LA) annotations. For cross-domain evaluation, we use CardiacUDA Yang et al. (2023) as an external target domain. Specifically, we use the public labe_all_frame subset, which provides dense frame-wise annotations suitable for full-sequence evaluation, whereas the remaining released subsets are sparsely annotated or, in some cases, unlabeled. We exclude volumes containing label codes outside the documented A4C label space, leaving eight valid full-frame patient volumes comprising 428 slices in total. Thus, the resulting cohort includes all usable volumes from the densely annotated subset under our preprocessing criteria rather than a manually selected sample. Because the public release does not provide a case-level manifest corresponding to its reported 8:1:1 split, we treat this cohort as a fixed external CardiacUDA subset rather than the complete official test partition. CAMUS and CardiacUDA share LV and LA labels, enabling direct evaluation of cross-domain generalization and test-time adaptation. (2023) . No identifiable patient information was accessed and no new human participants were recruited. Accordingly, no additional institutional review board approval or informed consent was required for this secondary analysis.

4.2 Implementation Details All experiments were implemented in PyTorch and conducted on an NVIDIA Blackwell PRO 6000 GPU. U-Net Ronneberger et al. (2015) , SwinUNETR Hatamizadeh et al. (2022) , MedSAM2 Ma et al. (2025) , and the supervised static-memory component of MemSeg-Agent were trained for 200 epochs with a batch size of 8. nnU-Net Isensee et al. (2021) followed its official configuration and was trained for 1000 epochs with a batch size of 2. AdamW was used with a learning rate of 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} and weight decay of 10 − 4 10^{-4} . MemSeg-Agent uses SAM2.1 Hiera-Tiny as the segmentation backbone. Its image encoder, memory encoder, memory attention, prompt encoder, and mask decoder remain frozen throughout training and deployment, such that only the static-memory variables are optimized during supervised memory construction. Few-shot and test-time working memories require no gradient-based optimization. Prediction uses an empty prompt, and a frozen DINOv3 encoder is used for similarity-based memory retrieval. Training and inference are performed slice-wise, while segmentation performance is evaluated after reconstructing three-dimensional volumes using the Dice similarity coefficient (Dice) for region overlap and the 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) for boundary accuracy. For clinician-triggered adaptation, target volumes are processed sequentially under the strict prequential protocol described in Section 3.5 . In retrospective experiments, clinician dissatisfaction is simulated using τ corr = 0.5 \tau_{\mathrm{corr}}=0.5 , while working-memory novelty is determined using τ sim = 0.95 \tau_{\mathrm{sim}}=0.95 . 4.3 Cross-Domain Working-Memory Adaptation In clinical deployment, models inevitably encounter domain shift when transferred to new scanners or imaging protocols. Continual segmentation methods address this through sequential parameter updates. We evaluate whether working-memory adaptation can offer an effective solution.

We compare MemSeg-Agent with the official Lifelong nnU-Net González et al. (2023) and UnCLeSAM Ranem et al. (2024) . We evaluate this setting by transferring models trained on CAMUS to the external CardiacUDA cohort and compare MemSeg-Agent with Lifelong nnU-Net González et al. (2023) and UnCLeSAM Ranem et al. (2024) . All methods are evaluated on the same target volumes using identical volume-level metrics. As shown in Table 2 , direct transfer yields macro-average Dice scores of 19.79%, 19.90%, and 15.57% for static-only MemSeg-Agent, Lifelong nnU-Net, and UnCLeSAM, respectively. With working-memory adaptation, MemSeg-Agent achieves 77.93% Dice and 9.90 mm HD95 on CardiacUDA, compared with 19.79%/44.02 mm for static memory alone, 19.90%/86.63 mm for Lifelong nnU-Net, and 15.57%/97.59 mm for UnCLeSAM. We evaluate whether static memory can serve as an equivalent substrate under varying annotation budgets (10%, 30%, 100% supervision) across three datasets, and whether memory-only exchange enables efficient federated collaboration across institutions. We demonstrate the performance of static memory in Table 1 and qualitative results in Fig. 2 .

We evaluate the same pseudo-observation memory parameterization with two frozen SAM2-family backbones: the default SAM2.1 Hiera-Tiny backbone and the official MedSAM2 backbone, respectively. Static memory remains competitive with fully trained segmentation models while keeping the backbone frozen. The memory formulation also supports federated learning settings. In the four-site FedAvg experiment, only the pseudo-observation memory is exchanged across sites. Since only a 2M-parameter memory is updated rather than the full 148.63M SAM2-tiny backbone, per-round communication is reduced by ∼ \sim 74.3 × \times ( ∼ \sim 98.65%) while maintaining competitive segmentation performance. 4.5 Working-Memory Accumulation and Consolidation We further evaluate how working memory accumulates deployment experience and whether similarity-aware consolidation can control memory growth during sequential adaptation from CAMUS to CardiacUDA. As shown in Table 3 , static memory alone achieves 31.16%/8.42% Dice for LV/LA. Static+Append improves performance to 83.10%/73.38%, while Static+Delta achieves comparable performance of 82.41%/73.45%. On the final five target volumes, Static+Delta achieves 81.12%/69.73% Dice, compared with 33.06%/4.79% for static memory alone. Meanwhile, Delta consolidation reduces the final working-memory size from 29/114 entries with append-only storage to 22/40 entries for LV/LA. We additionally visualize sequential adaptation under the CHAOS → \rightarrow ACDC shift in Fig. 4 , where segmentation performance improves as target-domain corrections accumulate in working memory. As shown in Fig. 5 , task-aligned memories, including pseudo-observations, direct memory tokens, and real examples, produce meaningful predictions, whereas unrelated-domain, label-shuffled, random, and empty memories yield near-zero Dice ( ≤ 0.26 % \leq 0.26\% ). Among the evaluated representations, direct memory tokens achieve the highest Dice, while pseudo-observations remain effective and preserve the shared SAM2-compatible memory interface used throughout MemSeg-Agent. Figure 3 (a) compares static-only, working-only, and combined memory, with the combined setting achieving the strongest overall performance across all evaluated datasets. Figure 3 (b) shows that fewer working-memory entries are sufficient when a related static prior is available, while performance benefits more from additional working memory when the static prior is unrelated. The same static-memory formulation also remains effective with a frozen MedSAM2 backbone, as reported in Table 1 , further supporting its applicability across different SAM2-family backbones.

5 Discussion Our results demonstrate that task- and domain-specific knowledge can be effectively represented and updated in the native memory space of a frozen segmentation foundation model. Under cross-domain deployment, all evaluated methods suffer substantial performance degradation under direct transfer from CAMUS to CardiacUDA; in contrast, incorporating target-domain corrections through working memory markedly improves subsequent segmentation without modifying the pretrained backbone, demonstrating that target-domain experience can be effectively accumulated in memory space. In supervised settings, static memory remains competitive across imaging modalities, anatomical regions, and annotation budgets, indicating that task-specific knowledge can be encoded outside the backbone parameters. And memory-only federated learning further extends this finding by substantially reducing per-round communication—approximately 74.3 × \times —through the exchange of only compact memory variables. During sequential deployment, delta-based consolidation achieves performance comparable to append-only storage with a smaller working-memory bank, indicating that redundant deployment experience can be compressed without loss. Finally, the ablation studies confirm that performance depends on task-relevant memory content, that static and working memories provide complementary sources of prior knowledge and deployment experience, and that the same static-memory formulation remains effective across SAM2-family backbones. Together, these findings support memory space as a shared substrate for knowledge acquisition, deployment-time adaptation, and reuse across different stages of the model lifecycle. Several limitations remain. First, clinician feedback is currently simulated retrospectively using ground-truth corrections. Real-world clinical validation has not yet been conducted. Therefore, the current results may not fully represent performance under realistic clinical feedback.

variability, or clinical correction time. Second, the current experiments use class-specific, slice-wise binary segmentation; extension to joint multi-class and three-dimensional segmentation requires further validation. Third, static-memory performance degrades under very limited supervision, partly due to only four patient volumes are available for static-memory training under the 10% supervision setting, which substantially limits the diversity and reliability of the learned task prior. Fourth, the controller is also lightweight and rule-based, and its retrieval thresholds and consolidation criteria may require adjustment across different deployment domains. Finally, the federated experiment demonstrates communication efficiency but does not provide formal privacy guarantees. Future work will evaluate the framework on larger multi-institutional cohorts with realistic clinician feedback, and extend memory-space adaptation to multi-class and volumetric segmentation with more adaptive retrieval and consolidation policies. Beyond medical segmentation, MemSeg-Agent suggests a different interpretation of test-time learning. Existing test-time training (TTT) and adaptation methods typically introduce fast plasticity by optimizing selected parameters, auxiliary modules, or other fast weights during deployment, while long-term knowledge remains encoded in slowly learned model parameters. Biological learning, however, does not exhibit a strict separation between training and inference. Instead, information is integrated over multiple timescales, with rapidly changing neural activity and transient memory traces supporting immediate behavior, while slower consolidation stabilizes selected experience into longer-term knowledge.

MemSeg-Agent conceptually follows this multi-timescale organization: the frozen foundation model provides a stable long-term prior, working memory serves as a rapidly editable substrate for incorporating sparse target-domain experience, and memory consolidation determines which information persists and influences subsequent cases. From this perspective, the central idea is not merely to replace parameter updates with a memory controller, but to move from weight-centric adaptation toward memory-centric learning, where fast adaptation, selective consolidation, and stable prior knowledge are represented as distinct but interacting mechanisms. This formulation may provide a broader direction for continual and test-time learning systems that remain plastic in changing environments, where adaptation knowledge accumulates in memory rather than overwrites the model itself. 6 Conclusion We introduced memory-space adaptation as a unified learning formulation for medical image segmentation, in which task knowledge and deployment experience are maintained through an explicit memory state while the foundation model remains fixed. MemSeg-Agent realizes this formulation through complementary static, few-shot, and working memories coordinated by a shared read–write process. Across supervised, continual, cross-domain, and federated settings, our results show that adaptation knowledge can be stored, accumulated, and reused effectively in memory space, supporting a more general view of learning that extends across different supervision levels and deployment stages. Future work will explore this paradigm in multi-class volumetric segmentation, larger multi-institutional cohorts, and prospective clinical settings with realistic and potentially noisy clinician feedback.
